lesson.title: Testing a Claim About a Single Proportion
lesson.summary: The one-proportion z-test checks whether a sample proportion provides convincing evidence against a claimed population proportion, using the null value p0, not the sample proportion, to compute the standard error.
lesson.body:
A test for one proportion asks whether a sample proportion, phat, computed from a random sample, is consistent with a claimed value of the population proportion, called p0. As with any hypothesis test, you start by stating a null hypothesis, H0: p = p0, and an alternative, Ha: p < p0, p > p0, or p not equal to p0, depending on what you are trying to show. The test statistic follows the same general structure as any test statistic: it standardizes the gap between what you observed and what the null hypothesis claims, measured in standard errors. For a proportion, that test statistic is z = (phat - p0) divided by the square root of p0(1 - p0)/n.

Here is the detail that trips up almost everyone the first time: the standard error in this formula uses p0, the null hypothesis value, not phat, the sample proportion. This is different from a confidence interval for a proportion, where phat is the best available estimate of the true proportion and so phat is used to build the standard error there. A hypothesis test, though, starts by assuming H0 is true, and it asks how surprising the observed phat would be if that assumption held. Since the test is conducted under the assumption that p really does equal p0, the standard error should reflect that assumed value, not the value you happened to observe in this particular sample. Using phat instead of p0 in a test statistic is a common mistake, and it is worth checking every time you set up this formula.

Suppose a company claims that 70 percent of its customers are satisfied with its service. A consumer group samples 150 customers at random and finds that 93 of them, phat = 93/150 = 0.62, report being satisfied. Does this sample give convincing evidence that the true satisfaction rate is below the company's claim. Set H0: p = 0.70 and Ha: p < 0.70, using alpha = 0.05. Under H0, the standard error is the square root of (0.70)(0.30)/150, which is the square root of 0.21/150 = 0.0014, or about 0.0374. The test statistic is z = (0.62 - 0.70) / 0.0374 = -2.14. The p-value, the probability of getting a sample proportion this low or lower if p really were 0.70, is P(Z < -2.14), which is about 0.016. Since 0.016 is less than alpha = 0.05, the sample provides convincing evidence that the true satisfaction rate is below the claimed 70 percent.

Before trusting this p-value, though, you need to check that the sampling distribution of phat is actually close enough to normal for the z-procedure to be trustworthy in the first place, which is exactly what the conditions for a z-test check next.
